full_judgment:
4. The trial court on consideration of the evidence came to the conclusion that accused Lalu committed the murder and convicted him under section 302 .B.P.C. He was sentenced to death. Accused Kabiruddin was convicted under sections 201 and 202 P.C. and sentenced to suffer R.I. for 7 years and sentenced to 6 months R.I. under section 302 P.C. and fine with direction that the sentences of Kabiruddin shall fun concurrently. 

 5. The trial court accepted the evidence of P.W. 3 Hafsa Khatun who deposed that the deceased was taken by accused Lalu and Kabir to Srimongal. P.W. 5 Ashokjan Bibi a sister of the deceased stated that the deceased went out with accused Lalu and Kabiruddin. So was the evidence of P.W. 6, husband of P.W. 5 P.W. 7 testified that he saw the deceased going to Srimongal with the two accused in a rickshaw. P.W. 10 Torab Ali saw that the deceased was going to Srimongal along with the two accused. P.W. 9 Profulla Kumar Das owner of a stationery shop at Srimongal town testified that there was a salish which was due to be held in his shop on 2.5.76 at 4 p.m. The deceased was also to attend the salish. But as he did not come at appointed time other salish members went away. Deceased came to the shop with accused Lalu and Kabir at 7 or 7.30 p.m. Thereafter the deceased went out of the shop. At that time the accused were in his verandah. In cross-examination he stated that when the deceased went out of the shop he did not see Lalu and Kabir. 

 6. Medical evidence by P .W. 8 shows an incised wound all round the neck at the upper level of the cricoid cartilage which completely separated head from the body with amongst other a punctured wound on the upper part of the abdomen on the midline just below xiphoid process measuring 2.5 x by cavity through huge quantity of small intestine with mesentery protruding. The opinion was that the injuries on the upper part of the neck correspond with the injuries on the lower part of the head and the neck and fits properly with the neck of the dead body including the colour and structure of the skill of both parts which indicates that the head and body of the same person. 

 9. The trial court found the confession is voluntary and he has implicated himself with regard to the hiding of the head and exculpated himself so far as the commission of the murder is concerned. In this view of the matter: the court accepted the inculpatory portion as true which received corroboration from his subsequent absconsion when on 18.5.76 he was arrested from the house of his father-in-law from a different village. The trial court noticed that the evidence on record proved that the deceased was last seen in the company of both the accused. Certain circumstances figured prominently such as in the following morning Lalu was no longer found in his home and the evidence shows that he had been to Bhanugach with an injury on his right hand. The trial court considered that the confessional statement of Lalu was also true and voluntary which reads as follows: 

 10. Considering the evidence and circumstances of the case both the accused were convicted and sentenced. On appeal the learned Judges of the High Court Division considered: 

 (d) the confessional statement of Kabiruddin is self exculpatory. This statement cannot be received in the evidence as confessional statement of an accused which could he used against the other accused. 

 (e) evidence of P.W. 18 and P.W. 21 is in conflict of evidence of P.W. 19, inasmuch as P.W. 19, did not notice any mark of injury in the right hand of accused Lab after his arrest and in this context considered the evidence of P.W. Hafsa Khatun who deposed that accused Lalu came to her house sometime between 10/11 p.m. and the learned Judges concluded presence of Lalu in the house of P.W. 3 "is capable of an explanation of the innocence of the accused." 

 (f) the evidence of P.W. 2 rickshaw-puller that accused Lalu, Kabir and the deceased boarded his rickshaw at Srimongal and he dropped them near the village road which met at the Dhaka-Srimogal road. The High Court Division did not place any reliance as P.W. 2 did not tell anybody of this fact for considerable period. 

 11. In this view of the case, the High Court Division considered that the prosecution failed to prove its case by conclusive circumstantial evidence as to the participation of the accused persons in the crime and as such the accused persons were given benefit of doubt. 

 13. Analysis of the evidence show that the deceased was last see a in the company of the two accused. P.Ws. 3, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 were uniform in their statement that they saw the deceased in company of the two accused in Srimongal bazar on the fateful night. The evidence of P.W. 9 is more specific and clear on this point. The F.I.R. was filed on 3.5.76 that is on the following day at about 9 O'Clock. It gives the vivid narration as to that the two accused took the deceased away from home to Srimongal Bazar. Be it noted that the F.I.R. was lodged by the informant before the discovery of the dead body. The circumstantial evidence of dragging of a blood stained body which ultimately led them to the bank of the tank ,covered by water-hyacinth was mentioned in the F.I.R. and the most significant fact that P.W. 9 Profulla saw them in the Srimongal bazar on the previous night was also mentioned. It is a circumstance of such a nature that must come for consideration while weighing the evidence. It is stated: 

 14. The circle is now full. That Profulla Kumar Das saw the accused with the deceased at about 9 P.M. is mentioned in the F.I.R. There is no hesitation in accepting the evidence that the two accused were in the company of the deceased and Profulla Kumar Das was last person who saw them together. Then the be-headed body was recovered from the tank at the instance of the police by P. W. 12. 

 Undoubtedly deceased Ashraf Ali was done to death. The question is who did it? We have discarded the evidence of P.W. 2, the rickshawwala, who claimed to have given a ride to the three persons, namely, two accused and the deceased, inasmuch as, he was neither examined by the police nor his evidence which was disclosed after 16 days would be a safe guidance for coming to a conclusion this way or any other. 

 Therefore only the oral evidence of the prosecution witnesses are to be considered. That evidence only shows that the deceased was last seen in the company of the accused and this is fully established by the evidence of P.W. 9. Now we are left with the circumstantial. evidence e.g. blood marks, marks of dragging etc. It is given by P.W. 1 who also mentioned these circumstances in the F.I.R. Oral evidence and circumstantial evidence only lead us up to the point that the deceased was in the company of the accused and thereafter the recovery of his dead body suggest that he had been done to death. As for the manner of the crime it is established that he had been injured and then dragged to the bank of the tank. Hence the question of confession comes for consideration. Both Lalu and Kabir made the confessional statements. Kabir confessed on 19.5.76, seventeen days after the occurrence and one day after his arrest. He was arrested from a different area from the house of his father-in-law. 

 15. The trial court took the correct view that in this statement “Kabir has only inculpated himself with regard to hiding of the head and exculpated himself so far as the commission of the murder is concerned," and in that view of the matter, the trial court accepted the inculpatory portion as true, inasmuch as, it is backed by the corroborative evidence from the subsequent conduct and absconsion. 

 16. The High Court Division, with respect, could not accept the subsequent conduct of absconsion by saying "their absence from their house is capable of a legitimate explanation." It is begging the question who is to give the explanation? Surely not the prosecution and then what explanation was given by the accused himself now? So the observation by the learned Judges that it is culpable of "a legitimate explanation" remains in the realm of conjecture. Now the question is how far the confessional statement of Kabir will be taken to adjudge as to the criminality of the matter Kabir in his statement mentioned that Lalu confided to him immediately after the marriage of the Member that he will kill him and sought his assistance in this regard whereupon Kabir declined to have anything to do in the matter and volunteered that he informed Lalu's father about this matter, who simply expressed his inability for doing anything in the matter. Notwithstanding this the evidence is that Kabir was in the company of Lalu on the fateful night. The exculpatory portion of the statement is improbable and false because knowing it full well that Lalu had made up his mind to finish the deceased no person could be in his company in such journey on the fateful night. The Member was an important man in the locality. Member was married on 17th Baisak, 1383 B.S. corresponding to 30th April, 1976 and the fateful journey was taken in the night of 2.5.76. Had it been the case that Lalu confided to finish the Member, Kabir would have disclosed it to others and inform the law enforcing authorities. He did not do so. Therefore it can be stated that the exculpatory portion is improbable and false. 

 17. Section 30 of the Evidence Act provides for consideration that a confession made by one of such persons affecting himself and some other of such persons being jointly tried and the Court may take into consideration such confession as against such other person as well as against the person who makes such confession the explanation says offence includes the abetment of or attempt to commit the offence. 

 18. It is unnecessary to go into long line of decisions which has firmly settled that such confessional statement can be taken into consideration in a limited manner. But it cannot be made the foundation of a conviction if there is no other reliable evidence tending to prove the guilt of the accused. The confession made by them can be used only in support of other evidence that is to corroborate the other evidence. Horwill J, In re Muthandi AIR 1242 Mad 444 held: 

 "If there is substantial evidence against the accused and there remains some lingering doubts, the confession of the accused may be taken into account to set that little doubt at rest." 

 "In the Allahabad case the question referred to the Full Bench was, whether the court could accept the inculpatory part of a confession which commended belief and reject the exculpatory part which was incredible. On reference to a large number of authorities cited the Full Bench observed that these authorities actually established no more than this that (a) where there is other evidence a portion of the confession may in the light of that evidence be rejected while acting: upon the remainder with the other evidence; and (b) where there is no other evidence and the exculpatory element is not inherently incredible, the court cannot accept the inculpatory element and reject the exculpatory element. 

 According to the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court the two rules above stated had been applied during the last one hundred years and the Full Bench answered the reference by holding where there is no other evidence to show affirmatively that any portion of the exculpatory element in the confession is false; the court must accept or reject the confession as a whole and cannot accept only the inculpatory element while rejecting the exculpatory clement is inherently incredible." This view was approved in the AIR 1952 (S.C.) 354 and in 1963 (3) (SCR) 678. 

 Section 30, however, provides that the court may take the confession into consideration and thereby, no doubt, makes it evidence on which the court may act; but the section does not say that the confession is to amount to proof. Clearly there must be other element in the consideration of all the facts proved in the case; it can be put into the scale and weighed with other evidence." 

 "The proper way to approach a case of this kind is first, to marshal the evidence against the accused excluding the confession altogether from consideration and see whether, if it is believed a conviction safely could be based on it. If it is capable of belief independently of the confession, then of course it is not necessary to call the confession in aid. But cases may arise where the judge is not prepared to act on the other evidence as it stands even though, if believed, it would be sufficient to sustain a conviction. In such an even t the judge may call in aid the confession and use it to lend assurance to the other evidence and thus fortify himself in believing what without the aid of the confession he would not be prepared to accept." 

 Stopping here for a moment, in the given case we have the evidence that (i) the deceased was last seen in the company of the two accused Lalu and Kabir, (ii) marks of violence have been found on the conjunction of Katcha and main road which led to the discovery of the dead body, (iii) dragging marks fit in with medical evidence that the fatal blow was given on the abdomen which caused the deceased to fall on the ground, (iv) injury marks on the hand of the deceased suggest that the victim intended to repulse the attack and injury mark on the hand of Lalu suggest that there was scuffle, and (v) and from the early morning of the following day both of them, being close: neighbours of the deceased were found absent from their respective homes and 15 days later accused Kabir was arrested from his father-in-law's house. These circumstances, namely, (a) last seen together in Srimongal bazar, (b) subsequent conduct and absconsion may cause an accusing finger to the accused but that is not enough for passing a conviction. Something more positive is required to fill up the gaps, inasmuch as, "there remains some lingering doubt" and as Horwill J said the confession of the accused may be taken into account to set that little doubt at rest. 

 "But cases may arise where the judge is not prepared to act on the other evidence as it stands even though, if believed, it would be sufficient to sustain a conviction. In such an event the judge may call in aid the confession and use it to lend assurance to the other evidence and thus fortify himself in believing what without the aid of the confession he would not be prepared to accept." 

 With respect, the law is thus formulated and the learned Sessions Judge had no hesitation in using the confessional statement of Kabir for sustaining the conviction. It is unfortunate in the appellate Judgment not a word has been said on section 30 of the Evidence Act and the learned Judges have focused only on section 24 without noticing that the two persons had been tried jointly and both of them had confessional statement to their credit. 

 21. Kabir said that he concealed the severed head. Wherefrom he got this head? The recovered be-headed body from the same tank showed that it fits on properly the neck of the dead body including the colour and texture of the skin on both parts which indicates that the head and body is of the same person (P.W. 8). If it is a head of the deceased Ashraf Ali as the evidence unmistakenable showed it to be so, then the question of body and its head comes for full consideration. The circumstantial evidence as given in the F.I.R. shows that the informant while looking for his brother noticed bleed stained earth near the conjunction of the village path and the Dhaka-Sylhet road and he noticed  কোন জিনিস টানিয়া নেওয়ার দাগ দেখা যায়। He followed trails of blood eventually came on bank of the tank. Injury No. 4 shows a punctured would on the abdomen of Ashraf Ali. Obviously he was given the deadly blow when he fell down on the ground and notwithstanding other injuries on his right forearm and right chest and right thumb, injury on the abdomen was deadly because huge quantity of intestine protruded. He was dragged and trails of blood bore, testimony, the cut marks on the right forearm and middle finger, injury Nos. 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 clearly show that the victim attempted to repulse the assailant and in the process the a assailant himself received injury in his right hand which led the trial court to conclude "it appears that the accused suffered injury in his right hand when there was resistance from the side of the deceased and the knife having slipped he himself was hurt. Therefore, the injury in his hand lends corroboration to his involvement in the crime. 

 23. Kabir stated that the statement was obtained by force and it was not voluntary. The evidence was given by the Magistrate that it was a voluntary statement and the trial court which had the advantage of seeing the witness and their demeanour accepted Kabir's confessional statement as voluntary. 

 24. Mr. Boktear Hossain, Advocate-on-record appearing for the State pointed out that Kabir was on bail for a considerable period during the 3 years between the date of his arrest and the trial and he obtained bail from the trial judge and never had made grievance that his statement was not voluntary and that it was obtained by force. The Evidence Act nowhere provides that a retracted confession cannot be taken into consideration against the co-accused or the confessing accused (See Ram Parkash V. S. AIR 1952 SC 1) 

 25. Lalu is the son of Jamat Ali and Kabir is the son of Kadar AIL Jamat Ali and Kadar Ali are the brothers of Ashabuddin Master, who died 3/4 years ago. His widow Hafsa Khatun was married by Jamat Ali, father of Lalu, but he divorced her after 2 years when deceased Ashraf Ali married her just 3 days before his murder. Lalu lives just adjacent to Hafsa Khatun P.W.3. Evidence was led that Hafsa Khatun had considerable land property তিন হাল জমি আছে।She stated in cross জায়গা সম্পত্তি রক্ষা করার জন্য আশ্বব মেম্বারকে বিয়ে করি। She further denied the suggestion সত্য নহে যে সম্পত্তি হস্তান্তর যাতে করতে না পারি সে জন্য লালুর বাপ আমাকে বিয়ে করে। She stated in chief আমার স্বামীর সম্পত্তি আসামীরা ও তাদের বাপেরা চাষাবাদ ও দেখাশুনা করত। 

 While in a criminal case the prosecution is not obliged to suggest any motive and the evidence that Is given in touch and go manner need not detain the court for speculating the motive of murder if otherwise the murder is proved by evidence and responsibility of it is proved beyond all reasonable doubt, the duty of the prosecution ends there, 

 26. It is reassuring to note the learned Sessions Judge when analyzing the evidence did not digress himself to these questions of side issues of motive. The prosecution case can be summarised in a tabloid form e.g. (i) deceased was last seen in the company of the accused, (ii) dragging mark on the road suggest the blow on abdomen was given on the road, (iii) cut mark on the hand of Lalu establishes his involvement, (iv) subsequent absconsion of the accused. 

 27. The evidence and the circumstances show the implication of the accused in the murder and without the confession a conviction could be recorded. The Sessions Judge merely took the confessional statement to fortify himself in believing what without the aid of the confession he would not be prepared to accept. "In other words whatever lingering doubt he had he took the statement to see that little doubt at rest." 

 28. Considering the facts and circumstances of this case there is no hesitation that the High Court Division had acquitted the accused on artificial reasons for giving benefit of doubt. The evidence unmistakably show that the prosecution has proved its case beyond all reasonable doubt. There is no escape from the conclusion that accused Lalu was the assailant, who caused the murder of deceased Ashraf Ali and accused Kabir committed the offence causing disappearance of the evidence and for withholding the information from law enforcing agency for which both of them were convicted by the trial court and rightly so. 

 31. Facts of the case, as already set forth in both the judgments, centre round the murder of Ashraf Ali, husband of P.W. 3, Hafsa Khatun, within 48 hours of their marriage which took place on 30 April 1976. Hafsa Khatun along with her minor son had inherited quite a big landed property from her first husband, Ashabuddin Master, paternal uncle of both the accused-respondents, Lalu Mia and Kabir. She alleged that she re-married the deceased, Ashraf Ali, who was an influential man, being a member of the Local Union Parishad, for protection of her property. Ashraf Ali left the house of Hafsa Khatun on the relevant day, 2-5-76, at about 5-30 P.M. for Sreemongal, about 2 miles away, accompanied by the two accused- respondents who were residents of the same homestead as of Hafsa Kbatun; he did not return home and on the following morning his dead body with the head completely severed was recovered from under the water-hyacinth of a pond about a quarter mile away from the house, near the village-path which connected the house with Dhaka-Sreemongal Trunk Road. Post-mortem examination of the dead body showed that it was a case of murder. The respondents were charged with the murder; they denied the charge and pleaded not guilty. The trial Court, Additional Sessions Judge, held Lalu guilty of murder and sentenced him to death and held Kabir guilty of causing the evidence of the murder to disappear by concealing the dead body and sentenced him to imprisonment for seven years with fine. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, on appeal, quashed their convictions and acquitted them both for want of satisfactory evidence to connect them with the crimes. Among the evidences adduced against them were two confessional statements, one by Lalu and the other by Kabir, but these were rejected by the High Court Division on the ground that the confession of Lalu was not voluntary and that of Kabir was exculpatory. 

 32. Apart from the confessional statements, evidence adduced by the prosecution consists of some circumstances only. They are: 

 33. In a case whose fate depends mainly on circumstantial evidence motive of the accused to commit the offence charged with is of fundamental importance, although in all other cases, such as, where the accused is sought to be connected with the offence by direct evidence, prosecution is not required to prove the. motive. In the instant case the charge brought against file accused is left to be proved by circumstantial evidence. P.W. 1, the informant and  P.W.3, Hafsa Khatun, attributed the motive to the landed property of Hafsa which was  managed, till her re-marriage with the member, by accused Lalu's father. Before the deceased,  Ashraf Ali, married her, Jamat Ali, father of Lalu, had married her to keep the property under his control, but owing to mal-treatment meted out to her by her co-wife, that is, mother of Lalu, the marriage ended in divorce, and since that time Lalu used to enter her hut very often forcibly. This matter was narrated by her to the member; she stated that for protection of her property she decided to marry the member. Hafsa was sought to be contradicted by the defence on the ground that she did not mention it to the Investigating-Officer or to the Magistrate. This appears to be a mere omission, for, it is the Defence, which itself proved the 'motive' by suggesting to her that after the death of her first husband she tried to sell out the landed property but was prevented from doing so by Lalu's father. Sudden introduction of a stranger in the person of the 'member', an influential man, obviously created an obstacle to management of the property by the accused. It is therefore clearly found that accused had a motive to commit the murder. 

 34. As to association of the respondents with the deceased, there are a number of' witnesses, such as P.Ws. 3,4, 5, 6, 7, and 10, but it is Hafsa's evidence which is sufficient to prove that her husband had left for Sreemongal in the company of the two accused a little before sunset. Again, that they were together in Sreernongal at about 7-30 P,M. has been testified to by P.W. 9, Profulla Das, a disinterested witness, who is a co-villager of the parties having a shop at Sreernongal Bazar. P.W. 2, a rickshaw puller, stated that these three persons, his next-door neighbours, had boarded his rickshaw at about 9 P.M. that night from Sreemongal on way home; his evidence deserves hardly any credit as he did not disclose this matter until after a fort-night and as his statement was not recorded by the Investigating Officer. Evidence of association as given by P.Ws. 3 and 9 does not by itself connect the accused with the murder, but it forms an important link with the murder, provided it is relied upon in the facts as given above. I see no reason why this evidence should not be relied upon. 

 35. As to the injury in the right-hand of Lalu, P.W. 18 Nikhil Ranjan Dey, a compounder has deposed that on 3-5-76 at about 1-30 P.M. a person went to his Pharmacy with his right hand wrapped with a gamcha and showed an injury in his right hand cutting all the fingers excepting the thumb whereupon he pushed an Injection and prescribed some medicine. This event was seen by a close neighbour of the compounder, P.W. 21 Ramkrishna Singha, who deposed that from his motor-car shop he saw a man who was given injection by the compounder at the same time and place. They identified accused Lalu as that man in court. Identification in court without first going through a test identification parade is an evidence which is very weak in nature. But in the instant case, it cannot be held so in view of the cut injury in the hand which was still clearly visible. When his attention was drawn by the trial Court while examining him under section 342 Cr. P.C., he give the explanation that during his childhood his fore-finger was cut. At this the Court looked at his fingers and found that the injury cut across the four fingers and reached the base of the thumb. This falsifies Lalu's explanation and corroborates the compounder's evidence. My learned brother, M.H. Rahman, J. has observed that examination of the injury-mark by the Court is inquisitorial in nature and as such is not admissible in evidence and support thereof has been sought from a decision of the Indian Supreme Court in Pre tam Singh vs. State of Punjab. AIR 1956 SC 415. 

 In that case the question was whether certain shoes recovered from the house of the accused fitted in his feet; the accused alleged that the shoes did not fit, but the trial Court after making some demonstration observed that the shoes so fitted. The Indian Supreme Court in that connection observed that the view or observation of the Court could not take the place of evidence. Fact of that case is so different that it hardly bears any comparison with the fact of the instant case. Whether a person got an injury mark in this hand can be tested just by a look at it, but whether a shoe fits in a person's foot can be best proved by its wearer: observation by other persons will be just an opinion and not a proof. In this case when a witness testified that he had seen an injury cutting four fingers of the accused on dock who however denied it, it is a duty of the court to look at the injury mark while examining the accused under section 342 Cr.P.C. 

 The Magistrate before recording a confessional statement of an accused must satisfy himself, by observing the demeanour of the prisoner and also questioning him, whether he is ready to make a confession voluntarily, free from any inducement, threat and intimidation: he must explain to the prisoner that he is not required to make a confession but if he makes any confession it might be used against him as evidence. The Magistrate should give him sufficient time for reflection and then again question him in a similar way and also assure him that whether he confesses or not, he will not be handed over to the police again, and if, by strictly observing these formalities, the magistrate believes that the prisoner in ready to make a confession voluntarily, then he will record it.' From the evidence of the Magistrate none of these requirements are found to have been fulfilled as he simply recorded the statement of the accused ignoring the broad fact that the accused was in police custody for six days, besides the complaint by him of torture. A confession of this nature can hardly be accepted as a voluntary one. The accused retracted the confession during trial. This confession is not found to be 'voluntary', and if a confession is not found to have been made voluntarily it must be rejected as inadmissible without entering into the question whether it is true. 

 38. Confession of accused Kabir, Ext. 2:  He was arrested by the police on 18-5-76 and was produced before the Magistrate P.W. 24 on,19-5-76, that is, within the shortest possible "time excluding the time spent during the journey from the place of arrest to the court. There the magistrate observed all the formalities, as stated above, and gave the prisoner three hours time for reflection. The magistrate deposed that he had cautioned the prisoner and explained to him that he was not required to make any confession, that in case he made a confession it might be used against him and that whether he made a confession or not he would not be remanded to the police custody, and that after questioning him and observing his demeanour he was satisfied that the prisoner was ready to make a statement voluntarily; then the accused made the confession which was recorded by the magistrate. This confession has been reproduced in the judgment of my learned brother B.H. Chowdhury, J, Substance of the statement is that one day after Hafsa's marriage with the 'member' accused Lalu told him the he would kill the member and wanted his assistance, which was however refused by him, the Kabir informed Lalu's father about the 'plan but the latter showed indifference to his sons affair, that he went to Sreemongal followed by Lalu and the member who were going there together, that after marketing when Lalu and the member boarded a rickshaw for returning home from Sreemongal, he was given a lift in the same rickshaw, that after proceeding some distance, they got down from the rickshaw, whose fare of Tk. 1.50 was paid by him (Kabir) that suddenly Lalu fell upon the member and killed him with a number of dagger blows ignoring his (Kabir) protest and concealed the body under water-hyacinth while he, (Kabir) at the order of Lalu, concealed the severed head under water-hyacinth. The trial Court rejected the exculpatory part of the statement as false and improbable and accepted the inculpatory part as evidence against him. The High Court Division rejected the confession as a whole as exculpatory. 

 40. In Pakala Narayan Swaami v. Emperor, AIR 1939 PC 47, Lord Atkin speaking for the Board observed: "A statement that contains self-exculpatory matter cannot amount to a confession if the exculpatory statement is of some fact which if proved would negative the offence alleged to be confessed. Moreover, a confession must either admit in terms the offence or at any rate substantially all the facts which constitute the offence." His Lordship then went into the question as to what is "confession" when the Evidence Act has not defined it. His Lordship disapproved of the definition of 'confession; given by Stephen in his Digest of the Law of Evidence as "an admission made by a person charged with a crime stating or suggesting the inference that he committed the crime." According to his Lordship "the inference that he committed the crime" is not sufficient to constitute a confession. But it should be noted that no confession, judicial or extra-judicial, was put in as evidence against the accused in that case but the question that arose there was whether a statement made by the accused before his arrest under section 167. Cr.P.C. to a police officer could be used against him in evidence. To appreciate the point a brief reference to the facts of the case will be necessary. 

 41. On 23 March 1937 the dead body of a man was found in a brand new steel-trunk in a railway compartment at Puri Railway Station. The dead body was identified later on as that of Kuree Nakuraju of Pithapur and, according to autopsy report; it was a case of murder. Accused Narayan Swami of Berhampur, about 250 miles from Pithapur, was charged with the murder and was found guilty. Conviction recorded by the Sessions Judge and confirmed in appeal by the Patna High Court rested on the following circumstances: (i) A statement made by the deceased to his wife in the morning of 21 March (1937) that he was going to Berhampur on invitation of the wife of the accused to receive his dues; (ii) a number of letters and notes written by the wife of the accused to the deceased from whom she. had borrowed money at different times in small amounts totalling Rs. 3000/- on promise to repay with interest: (iii) the deceased was a peon in the service of the Dewan of Pithapur about 20 years ago and the wife of the accused was the Dewani's daughter and when she was a girl of about 14 she had developed intimacy with the deceased; (iv) a statement of the accused to the police before his arrest admitting that the deceased had come to his house on 21 March and left in the following morning; (V) the steel trunk which contained the dead body had been purchased by a servant of the accused on 22 March: (vi) testimony of a Jetka driver that in his jetka the accused had loaded a steel trunk, like the questioned one, which he carried to the Railway Station on 23 March; (vii) testimony of a respectable person that he had seen the accused at the Railway Station on 23 March. Before the Board admissibility of only two of these circumstances were challenged, one was the statement of the deceased made to his wife about the circumstances that led to his death and the other was the alleged statement of the accused made to the police that the deceased had come to his house. Their Lordships rejected the contention of the appellant as to the statement of the deceased and held it admissible under section 32(1) of the Evidence Act, but accepted the contention of the appellant that his alleged statement or admission to the police was hit by section 162 Cr.P.C. This statement was excluded from consideration but the conviction was upheld on the basis of other materials as shown above. Section 162 Crl.P.C. provides that no statement made by "any person" to a police officer in the course of an investigation shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it, nor any part thereof shall be used for any purpose except for the purpose of contradicting its maker when he deposes in court as prosecution witness. In that case it was contended by the respondent that "any person" in section 162 Cr.P.C. does not include an accused person or a person who subsequently becomes an accused and that the statement of the accused to the police admitting that the deceased had come to his house was rightly used as evidence against him. It is in these circumstances that their Lordships of the Privy Council made the observation that a statement of an accused containing exculpatory matter does not amount to confession. 

 The trial Court a Special Magistrate, acquitted both the accused from the charge of criminal conspiracy for forgery for want of evidence, but convicted both of them on the other two charges, that is, forging the documents P-3 and P-24. The conviction was maintained in appeal by the Sessions Judge whereupon the matter was brought before the High Court in revision but to no effect. Then the matter was brought before the Supreme Court by special leave. There the convictions under both the charges were quashed and the appellants were acquitted. Ground for quashing the conviction in respect of Ext. P-3 is that this conviction was recorded mainly on uncorroborated testimony of an interested person, the Office Superintendent (P.W. 13) who deposed that accused No. 1 had taken home all the sealed tenders. 

 As to the third charge, relating to document Ext. P-24. an admission of the ace- used was involved. Ext. P-24 is a letter bearing the date "2011-46". The prosecution alleged that it was an ante-dated document having been written and dated sometime in August 1947. It was a letter admittedly written by Patel, accused No. 2, to the Excise Commissioner, accused No. 1. It was stated therein that about a week ago he (Patel) went to the house of Assistant Commissioner, Amarnath and found Doongaji sitting with the Assistant Commissioner; he also found his tender along with other tenders 'opened' and lying on Amar Nath's table. He got astonished and suspected foul play and apprehended that the matter of tenders was going to be manipulated in favour of Doongaji. He in this letter dated 20-11-46" brought this matter to the notice of the Commissioner of Excise seeking justice and fair play. This letter bore an endorsement of accused No. 1 bearing the date "21-11-46" to the effect that "No action necessary. File This letter was not kept in the appropriate File but was discovered in August 1947 in the midst of other papers. It was alleged by the prosecution that this letter was written after the accused got scent of the enquiry started by the Anti-Corruption Police and was intended to direct the course of inquiry to a wrong channel, against Amarnath and Doongaji, for ultimate benefit of the accused. Evidence in support of this charge was that the letter, in the opinion of an Expert witness, Was not typed on the typewriter machine Art. Ext. B as claimed by accused No. 2, but was typed on the typeriter machine Art. Ext. A, which along with other type-writers of this brand, was supplied to this place, Nagpur, after 31-12-46 and that the figure 6 of the date of the letter "20-11-46" was penned through and replaced with the figure 7. The Supreme Court held that opinion of the expert that a particular letter was typed on a particular machine does not fall within the ambit of Section 45, Evidence Act, and is inadmissible ; and as to the replacement of figure' 7' by figure '6' by over-writing, the Court held that the alteration of the date was not unusual but was by way of correction of a mistake by inadvertence. The charge was therefore left to be proved by a statement of accused Patel under section 342 Cr.P.C. in which he indicated that the letter was not typed on Art. Ext. B but might have been typed on any other typewriter machines which were brought by his office for "trial". His statement under section 342 Cr.P.C. was in the following words: 

 "If the evidence of the expert is eliminated, there is no material for holding that Ext. P-24 was typed on Art. A. The trial Magistrate and the learned Sessions Judge used part of the statement of the accused for arriving at the conclusion that the letter not having been typed on Art. B must necessarily have been typed on Art. A. Such use of the statement of the accused was wholly unwarranted. It is settled law that an admission made by a person whether amounting to a confession or not cannot be split up and part of it used against him. An admission must be used either as a whole or not at all. 

 43. In Nishi Kanta Jha v. State of Bihar, AIR 1969 SC 422, the exculpatory part of a confession of the accused was disbelieved and rejected by the court and its inculpatory part was accepted and the conviction of the accused for murder was upheld by the Supreme Court in view of the facts and circumstances of that case which are briefly stated here for better appreciation of the point involved: From a first class railway compartment of the Barawni Express a dead body of a person with multiple stab- injuries was recovered when the train reached Madhabpur Railway Station at about 4 P.M., on 12-10-61, and about two hours thereafter, a person was found washing his blood stained clothes in a river; there was a cut-injury in his right fore-finger. On query by a passer-by (P.W. 17) he explained that a cow-boy had caused the injury with a glass in the course of a sudden quarrel. The witness, ongoing home, reported the matter to his brother (P.W. 24) who stated that he heard just a while ago that the dead body of a person had been recovered at the Railway Station and that the murderer had been missing. P. W. 24, along with others, went out in search of the man and having found him a few miles away arrested him and then produced him before the village head-man to whom he made a statement. In the statement he admitted his presence in the First Class Railway Compartment in which a murder was committed. He disclosed his identity as Nishi Kanta Jha and stated that when he boarded the Express train at Jhajha Railway Station he found "an unknown 'passenger" in the First Class compartment, that from the next station, Sirutala, one Lalmohan Sharma, whom he knew from before, entered the compartment, that when the train left the next station Lalmohan Sharma killed the 'unknown passenger' by several dagger blows and when he tried to prevent the assaults he received the cut-injury in his right hand, that when the train reached the next Railway Station, Madhabpur, Lalmohan Sharma left the train and finding himself alone in the compartment, along with the murdered man, he also jumped down in fear of arrest. He further stated that he washed his blood stained clothes in a river and proceeded to the house of his cousin at Roshan but was apprehended by P. W. 24 and others who produced him to the head-man. During trial the evidence particularly of the Headmaster of Jhajah High School. disclosed that the victim was Joy Prakash Dobe, a student of Class X (Science Group) of his school and the accused, Nishikanta, was a student of the same school and same class but in Art Section and that both of them played foot-ball in the school. The question arose whether this confessional statement could be used against the accused since it was exculpatory in nature excepting the admission of his innocuous presence in the railway compartment as a passenger witnessing the crime committed by one Lalmohan Sharma. If his statement excepting his presence in the compartment was excluded there was no evidence to connect him with the murder, merely on the basis of the cut injury in his finger. He was convicted by the High Court which accepted the inculpatory part of the statement and rejected the exculpatory part as false and inherently improbable and his conviction was maintained in appeal by the Supreme Court on the following reasons: The exculpalory portion was inherently improbable particularly, a minor cut-injury in the fore-finger could not have caused profuse bleeding flooding his entire clothes, exercise books and was also contradicted by the explanation of the accused under section 342 CrI.P.C. wherein he stated that he had not travelled by the Barauni Express but he had travelled by the Too- fan Express which had reached Madhabpur Station about four hours earlier, that the injury in his finger was inflicted by cow-boy while he was proceeding to Roshan after getting down from the train. 

 The trial Court however did not convict him for the murder but convicted him for concealment of the dead body obviously because the confession which was retracted during trial got no corroborating evidence in his case excepting the evidence of association. The evidence as to motive is mainly attributed to accused Lalu. 

 The evidence of association, motive and the cut-injury in the hand connects Lalu with the crime. In addition the confession of Kabir in respect of concealment of the dead body at the same time and place may be considered against Lalu under section 30 of the Evidence Act as both of them were tried together for commission of the same offence. In view of these facts and circumstances convictions recorded against both of them by the trial Court are restored with the modification that the sentence of Lalu is commuted to that of transportation for life. 

 47. The Trial Court convicted respondent No. 1 Lalu under section 302 and respondent No. 2 Kabiruddin under sections 201 and 202 of the Penal Code after considering the following circumstantial evidence: 

 49. Retraction of a confession at an earliest opportunity may lend support to the defence plea that the confession was not voluntary one, but from a belated retraction of a confession no inference adverse to the accused can be made. When an accused says that he did not make the confession that amounts to retraction. An accused may be convicted even on a retracted confession if it is inculpatory but corroboration is required. But this rule of prudence, however, does not require. (as has been pointed out in Hemraj vs. State of Ajmer A.I.R 1954 SC 462 and in Balbir Singh Vs. State of Punjab AIR 1957 SC 216) that each and every circumstance mentioned in the confessional statement must be separately and independently corroborated then the rule will be meaningless as an independent evidence itself would afford sufficient basis for conviction and it would be unnecessary to call the confession in aid. More on confession later. 

 50. This appeal by special leave against the Appellate Court's order of acquittal calls for close scrutiny of the prosecution case. More often than not a case of circumstantial evidence starts with a motive. The instant case is no exception. P.W. 1  stated that after arriving at the place of the recovery of the dead body P. W. 3 Hafsa said that the accused’s and their fathers had been forcibly enjoying her property and that in their apprehension that her marriage with the deceased might affect their interest adversely the accused killed her husband. P.W. 3 Hafsa herself stated that the accused and their fathers used to cultivate and manage her property and they thought they would be deprived if she got married to the Member. She however, admitted in cross that she did not say so either before the Magistrate before whom she made a statement or before the police. At the trial she did not say that the accused killed her husband. This fact should not be lost sight of.

None of the other witnesses, the deceased's other wife (P.W. 4), sister (P.W. 5), brother (P.W. 15), brother-in-law (P.W. 10 ), made any such allegation against the accused nor did any of them corroborate P.W. 1 that at place of the recovery of the dead body P.W. 3 Hafsa stated that the accused killed her husband. The deceased married Hafsa on Friday 30th April, 1976. Hafsa states that the accused Lalu arranged that marriage. P.W. 1 states that Lalu signed the marriage-contract. The deceased was done to death two days after the marriage. There is no evidence that there was a quarrel between Lalu and the deceased within those two days. P.W. 1 states in cross that he did not know of any golmal (hitch) between the accused and Hafsa over the latter's property. Apart from the alleged confessions there is absolutely no evidence to indicate a desire for vengeance against the deceased in the minds of the accuseds arranged that marriage. PW1 states that Lalu signed the marriage contract. The deceased was done to death two days after the marriage. There is no evidence that there was a quarrel between Lalu and the deceased within those two days. PW1 states in cross that he did not know of any golmal (hitch) between the accused and Hafsa over the latter's property. Apart from the alleged confessions there is absolutely no evidence to indicate a desire for vengeance against the deceased in the minds of the accuseds. 

 52. It is true that in criminal trial the question of motive is of very little importance when there is direct and reliable evidence to prove the crime. But in a case that depends solely on circumstantial evidence, as in this case, the proof of motive would form one of the links, the first link in the chain of circumstantial evidence, and an absence of reliable proof as to motive itself becomes a relevant factor in considering the evidence relating to incriminating circumstances alleged against the accused. See Rajinder Kumar and another vs State of Punjab AIR 1966 SC 1322 and Shivji Genu Mohite vs State of Maharashtra AIR 1973 SC 55.

The fact that the accused absconded soon after the crime may only lend weight to other evidence. In Thimma vs State of Mysore AIR 1971 SC 1871 (1877) it is correctly pointed out that "Even innocent persons may, when suspected of grave crimes, be tempted to evade arrest: such being the instinct of self preservation in an average human being".

 62. There is another serious flaw in the prosecution case, PW 18 and PW 21 did not know the accused Lalu from before. Identification of Lalu at the court by these two witnesses for the first time without being preceded by test identification parade cannot be acted upon to convict the accused. In Budhsen and another vs State of UP AIR 1970 SC 1321 it is held that the evidence of mere identification of the accused person at trial for the first time is from its very nature inherently of a weak character. In Rameshwer Singh vs State of Jammu and Kashmir AIR 1972 SC 102 (104) it is held that "the substantive evidence of a witness is his evidence in court but when the accused person is not previously known to the witness concerned then identification of the accused by the witness soon after the former's arrest is of vital importance because it furnishes to the investigating agency an assurance that investigation is proceeding on right lines in addition to furnishing corroboration of the evidence to be given by the witness later in court at the trial. From this point of view it is a matter of great importance both for the investigating agency and for the accused and a fortiori for the proper administration of justice that such identification is held without avoidable and unreasonable delay after the arrest of the accused and that all the necessary precautions and safeguards are effectively taken so that the investigation proceeds on correct lines for punishing the real culprit. It would, in addition, be fair to the witness concerned who was a stranger to the accused because in that event the chances of his memory fading are reduced and he is required to identify the alleged culprit at the earliest possible opportunity after the occurrence". 

 "The learned Additional Sessions Judge was certainly not entitled to allow his view or observation to take the place of evidence because such view of observation could not be tested by cross-examination and the accused would certainly be not in position to furnish an explanation in regard to the same." 

 67. Confession is a species of admission. Sections 24 to 30 of the Evidence Act and sections 162 and 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure govern the law relating to confession. A confession or admission is evidence against its maker, unless its admissibility is excluded by provisions embodied in the Evidence Act. As the term confession was not defined in that Act the Courts in this Sub-continent adopted Stephen's definition of confession given in his Digest of the Law of Evidence. Stephen defined confession as an admission made at any time by a person charged with crime stating or suggesting the inference that he committed a crime. Straight, J, in R vs Jagrup, (1885) ILR 7 All 646 and Chandawarkar, J in R vs Santya Bandhit, (1909) II Bom LR 633, however, did not accept such a wide definition and gave a narrower meaning to the expression 'confession' holding that only a statement which was a direct acknowledgement of guilt would amount to confession and did not include merely inculpatory admission which falls short of being admission, of guilt. Confusion as to the meaning of 'confession' was noted by the Privy Council in Pakala Narayana Swami vs The King Emperor, AIR 1939 PC 47(52). Lord Atkins observed that "no statement containing self-exculpatory matter could amount to confession, if the exculpatory statement was of some fact, which if true could negative the offence alleged to be confessed. Moreover, a confession must either admit in terms the offence, or at any rate substantially all the facts which constitute the offence. An admission of a gravely incriminating fact even a conclusively incriminating fact, is not itself a confession i.e., an admission that the accused is the owner of and was in recent possession of the knife or revolver which caused death with no explanation of any other man's possession. Some confusion appears to have been caused by the definition of confession in Article 22 of Stephen's Digest of the Law of Evidence which defines a confession as an admission made at any time by a person charged with crime stating or suggesting the inference that he committed that crime. If the surrounding articles are examined, it will be apparent that the learned author after dealing with admissions generally is applying himself to admissions in criminal cases, and for this purpose defines confessions so as to cover all such admissions, in order to have a general terms for use in the three following articles, confession secured in inducement, made upon oath, made under a promise of secrecy. The definition is not contained in the Evidence Act, 1872; and in that Act it would not be consistent with the natural use of language to construe confession as a statement by an accused "suggesting the inference that he committed" the crime." 

 68. In Hanumant Govind vs State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1952 SC 343 it was held that "It is settled law that an admission made by a person whether amounting to confession or not cannot be split up and part of it used against him. An admission must be used either as whole or not at all." On this Mitter J. observed in Nishikant Jha vs State of Bihar AIR 1969 SC 422 at page 429 that was not the ratio decidendi in the facts and circumstances of that case. In Palvinder Kaur vs State of Punjab AIR 1952 SC 354 it was, however, reiterated that the court cannot accept the inculpatory part of a statement and reject the exculpatory part. In that case a reference was made to the decision of the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court in Balmakund vs Emperor AIR 1931 All 1 where it was held that "where there is no other evidence to show affirmatively that any portion of the exculpatory element in the confession is false; the court must accept or reject the confession as a whole and cannot accept only the inculpatory element while rejecting the exculpatory element as inherently incredible". 

 "From that isolated observation, it is difficult to say whether he (Shah J.) widened the definition than the one given by the Privy Council. But he did not include in the expression 'confession' an admission of a fact, however, incriminating which by itself would not be enough to prove the guilt of the crime in question, although it might, together with the other evidence on record, lead to the conclusion of the guilt of the accused persons." 

 71. In Aghnoo Nagasia vs State of Bihar AIR 1966 SC 119 at page 123 Bachawat, J, after referring to Lord Atkin's observations in Pakala Narayana Swami's case and their approval in Palvinder Kaur's case, defined a confession as "an admission of the offence by a person charged with offence." After reiterating the views expressed in Hanumant's case, Bachawat J observed, by way of elaboration, that "a confession may consist of several parts and may reveal not only the actual commission of the crime but also the motive, the preparation, the opportunity, the provocation the weapons used, the intention, the concealment of the weapon and the subsequent conduct of the accused. If the confession is tainted, the taint attaches to each part of it. It is not permissible in law to separate one part and to admit it in evidence as a non-confessional statement. Each part discloses some incriminating fact, i.e. some fact which by itself or along with other admitted or proved facts suggests the inference that the accused committed the crime, and though each part taken singly may not amount to a confession, each of them being part of a confessional statement partakes of the character of a confession. If a statement contains an admission of an offence, not only that admission but also every other admission of an incriminating fact contained in the statement is part of the confession." 

 72. Then there came a change in the thinking of the Indian Supreme Court on the dichotomy of a confessional statement. After referring to Article 725 of Taylor's Law of Evidence (Eleventh Edition page 502), Roscoe's Criminal Evidence (Sixteenth Edition page 52) and Archihold's Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice (Thirty-Sixth Edition page 428) the Indian Supreme Court held in Nishikant Jha vs State of Bihar AIR 1969 SC 422 that it is permissible to believe one part of a confessional statement, and to disbelieve another, and it is open to the court to reject the exculpatory part which is found to be false and to take inculpatory part into consideration if there is other evidence to prove its correctness. That decision was followed in Bhagwan Singh Rana vs State of Haryana AIR 1975 SC 1797, Keshoram Bora vs State of Assam AIR 1978 SC 1096, Mohan Lai vs Ajit Singh AIR 1978 SC 1183. 

 73. A witness may tell, on oath or affirmation, that he will tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth. An accused may, in remorse or penitence, say he will disclose the whole thing and will make a clean breast of all that he did. In fact, however, despite the apparent seriousness of oath or affirmation by the witness or the gnawing sense of remorse in the mind of the accused, depositions and confessions are often found mixed up with truth and untruth. This is for various reasons. It may be due to forgetfulness, inadvertence, ignorance or lack of care or because of falsehood, deliberately designed. So far as assessment of evidence in, criminal trial is concerned the principle falsus in uno falsus in omnibus will not apply and the court has a duty to disengage truth from falsehood. In case of evaluating a confession, however, a process of reasoning by inference will not be adequate. The court's first duty is to consider the confession as a whole. It cannot reject an exculpatory part of a confession by inferential reasoning. It can only do so when there is clear evidence to show that the exculpatory part is false. Similarly the Court can act on an inculpatory part, even retracted, only when it is in accord with other evidence on record. 

 74. About the confession of a co-accused. Considering section 30 of the Evidence Act the Privy Council held in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King AIR 1949 PC 257 (259): This section was introduced for the first time in the Evidence Act, and marks a departure from the Common Law of England. It will be noticed that the section applies to confessions, and not to statements which do not admit the guilt of the confessing party....But a confession of a co-accused is obviously evidence of a very weak type. It does not indeed come within the definition of "evidence" contained in section 3 of the Evidence Act. It is not required to be given on oath, nor in the presence of the accused, and it cannot be tested by cross-examination Section 30, however, provides that the court may take the confession into consideration and thereby, no doubt makes it evidence on which the court may act; but the section does not say that the confession is to amount to proof. Clearly there must be other evidence. The confession is only one element in the consideration of all the facts proved in the case; it can be put into the scale and weighed with the other evidence." 

 75. Similar view was held in Maqbool Hussain vs The State 12 DLR (SC) 217 and is re-stated by this Court in Lutfun Nahar vs State 27 DLR (AD: 29, and the State vs Fazu Kazi, 29 DLR (SC) 271. In Joygun Bibi vs The State 12 DLR (SC) 156 it is held that the retraction of a confession is a circumstance which has no bearing whatsoever upon the question whether in the first instance it was voluntarily made, and on the further question whether it is true. It is further observed that such retraction becomes wholly immaterial once it is found that it was voluntary as well as true, but even then, it is held that a conviction cannot be sustained on such confession alone. The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction of Joygun Bibi, the appellant, as there was other evidence which along with the retracted confession of the co-accused pointed to her guilt. 

 76. In Balbir Singh vs Punjab State AIR 1957 SC 216 it is held so far as the confessional statement of one accused is concerned, it may be taken into consideration against the other accused if it fulfills the conditions laid down in section 30 of the Evidence Act One of the conditions is that the confession must implicate the maker substantially to the same extent as the other accused person against whom it is sought to be taken into consideration. 

 78. The appellant's contention that the High Court Division rejected Kabir's confession by observing in one sentence that it was exculpatory is not correct. The High Court Divisions considered that by his confession Kabir "has not incriminated himself or made any statement as to his participation in the crime. He has stated about his participation in some secondary acts and the alleged concealing of the head under water-hyacinth of the tank. The statement of this accused that he was picked up in the Bazar (Srimongal) by the deceased and the accused Lalu on their way to home is in conflict with fhe evidence of PW 2. Be that as it may, this statement cannot be received in evidence as a confessional statement of the accused which could be used against the other accused. But if this statement is found to be true the maker of this statement could however be convicted." 

 79. The accused Kabir in his retracted confession sought to exculpate himself both from the offence of murder as well as for the offence of concealing the evidence of murder. The Trial Court found the first portion exculpatory as there was no evidence to show that it was false. Kabir's admission that he was present at the place of occurrence cannot be termed as a confession of a co-accused and as he did not implicate himself substantially to the same extent as the accused Lalu with whom he was jointly charged for murder. Hence Kabir's such admission cannot be used under section 30 of the Evidence Act against the co-accused. Besides, there is no other independent corroborative evidence to convict the co-accused Lalu under section 302 of the Penal Code on that admission of Kabir. I have already stated that there, was no satisfactory evidence that the deceased was seen last in the company of the accused and that learned trial judge's examination of the injury in Lalu's right hand is not permissible in law. 

 80. This case is distinguishable from Nishi Kant Jha's case and the cases reported in AIR 1976 SC 1997 and AIR 1978 SC 1096 and at page 1183. In those cases there was no co-accused and the conviction was upheld because the exculpatory part was found to be patently false and the inculpatory part of the statement of the accused himself was in accord with other evidence on record. 

 81. About Kabir's conviction under sections 201 and 202 of the Penal Code. To constitute an offence under section 201 the accused must be proved to have actively participated in the matter of causing disappearing of evidence. As Kabir's act was not voluntary it cannot be termed as intentional. He acted by sufferance out of fear of Lalu who threatened him that he would liquidate him if he made any fuss about the murder. 

 83. After assessing the probabilities of the truth or falsehood of Kabir's retracted confession if any part of his statements is found to be inculpatory, even then there is no other corroborative evidence in record to sustain his conviction either under section 201 or under section 202 of the Penal Code. 

 84. In this case the answer to the question who killed Ashraf Ali is lost, like a needle in a haystack, beyond recovery in a mess of evidence of very suspicious nature. When this kind of prosecution case involving a heinous crime fails for the investigator's lack of care, intelligence and basic functional knowledge of criminal law men, looking for peace, law and order in the society, may get impatient and frustrated with the supposedly annoying complexities of laws of evidence and procedure, and feel that those laws of colonial days are worth a good riddance. The remedy, though, lies in the improvement of the quality of investigation. The provisions of the Evidence Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure—particularly with regard to the confession of an accused, recording of a confession by a Magistrate, and identification of the accused before a test identification parade by a witness not previously known to the accused—are based on grounds of public policy and on sound principles of jurisprudence which need not be jettisoned for lightening the burden of investigation, however onerous it may appear an occasions.
